extracted.intended_audience: policy analysts, patent statisticians, IP office staff, researchers and policymakers interested in patenting trends
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis and interpretation of patent system indicators (filings, grants, PCT use, patent families, field specialization and normalization metrics) for cross-country and technology comparisons. Provides definitions, caveats and guidance for using each indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Share of countries in total non-resident grants
rubrics_metrics.description: Share of countries in total non-resident patent grants (by country of origin) and their ranking over time (e.g., Japan, USA, Germany shares; emerging countries' low ranking).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation notes: Emerging countries such as Brazil, China, India and Mexico have a low ranking for non-resident grants by country of origin compared to their ranking by patent office — indicating low patenting activity abroad and a high presence of foreign applicants in their domestic markets. Between 2000 and 2006, Japan’s share increased while that of the USA and UK decreased; the combined share of the top eight countries remained roughly constant.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT filings: totals and growth rates
rubrics_metrics.description: Total number of PCT filings (international applications filed through the Patent Cooperation Treaty) and annual growth rates (trends 1985–2007, annual % growth series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation notes: Total PCT filings in 2007 ~158,400 (5.9% increase from previous year). PCT filings grew rapidly until 2001 (yearly growth >10%) then slowed. Country shares: the USA is the largest user (33.6% in 2006), Japan second (17.5% in 2006). Between 2000 and 2006, shares increased for Japan, Republic of Korea and China and decreased for the USA.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT filings by country of origin (share)
rubrics_metrics.description: Share of total PCT filings attributable to each country of origin (used to rank users of the PCT system).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: In 2006, 33.6% of all PCT filings originated from the USA, ~double the share of Japan. Filings from India, Austria, Spain and Italy are relatively low but increasing. Use these shares to identify largest users and changes over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution of PCT filings by ownership type
rubrics_metrics.description: Breakdown of PCT filings by ownership sector (business, university, government, others) and variation across countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: the distribution is calculated based on the top 3,000 PCT applicants and therefore may overstate the business sector (excludes individual filers and applicants with fewer than 5 filings). Observations: majority of PCT filings originate from business sector (varies by country from 99% in Sweden/Germany to 52% in Spain). University sector has high shares in Israel (19.9%), Australia (17.5%), Spain (15.2%); government sector >30% in Spain and India. Top 20 university applicants are from US and Japan; University of California is largest single university PCT applicant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of foreign filing route: direct vs PCT
rubrics_metrics.description: Indicator of non-resident filings split by direct national filings and filings via the PCT route (shares and trends over time, e.g., 1995–2006).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation and procedural note: To file in a foreign country, applicants may file directly or via PCT; foreign filings must be made within the 12-month Paris Convention priority period. Between 1995 and 2006, share of non-resident filings via PCT increased from 25.0% to 48.9%. Use varies by office: >85% of non-resident filings at Brazil, Indonesia, Philippines, Thailand, Norway and Mexico are via PCT; <20% in Germany, USA and UK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of foreign-oriented patent families
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent families defined as groups of patent applications filed with at least one foreign patent office (i.e., 'foreign-oriented families').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use and interpretation: Foreign-oriented patent families provide an indication of inventions that applicants consider worth protecting in multiple countries. Because families are based on first-filed applications they better reflect the number of distinct inventions (eliminates multiple counts) compared to raw counts of filings which can over-estimate inventions due to multiple filings for same invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat on counting by IPC/fields of technology (multiple IPCs per application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Mapping of International Patent Classification (IPC) symbols to fields of technology and counting rules when applications have multiple IPC symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because a patent application may be assigned multiple IPC symbols linked to different fields, the sum of patent filings by fields of technology is higher than the total number of filings. Annual growth by field should be interpreted with this overlap in mind. See annex B for concordance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative Specialization Index (RSI)
rubrics_metrics.description: RSI measures a country's relative concentration/specialization in particular technology fields, correcting for country size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definition and interpretation: A positive RSI value for a technology implies the country has a relatively high (above-average) share of patent families in that technology; a negative RSI implies below-average concentration. RSI corrects for country size and focuses on concentration. Use RSI based on foreign-oriented patent families to indicate R&D strength in specific fields (examples provided: Denmark and USA in biotechnology; India in pharmaceuticals; Finland/China/ROK/Sweden in telecommunications; Canada/Finland in IT; Singapore/ROK in semiconductors). See annex C for detailed RSI indicators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents filed by field of technology (fields list and trends)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classification of patent filings into major technology fields (I Electrical engineering, II Instruments, III Chemistry, IV Mechanical engineering, V Other fields) with subfields and counts/trends.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes: IPC symbols are linked to these fields by concordance (annex B). Report highlights: electrical engineering (including computer technology, telecoms, electrical machinery) is most active; optics and medical technology also have high filings. Growth observations: computer technology, optics and semiconductors grew strongly 2001–2005; IT methods for management, analysis of biological materials, and chemical engineering decreased in same period. Annual growth rates shown and should be interpreted per-field.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technology-specific indicators (energy technologies example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Domain-specific patent filing counts and country-of-origin distributions for energy technologies (solar, fuel cell, wind), defined via IPC symbols.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: Solar and fuel cell filings mainly originated from Japan; wind energy filings were more evenly distributed with Germany and Japan top. Total filings in wind energy considerably less than solar/fuel cell. Use IPC-based definitions (annex B) to identify domain filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident patent filings per GDP (normalization metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratio of resident patent filings to Gross Domestic Product (GDP) to correct for country size and improve comparability across countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notes and interpretation: GDP used is in billions of constant US$ PPP. This ratio reduces country-size effects compared to raw filing counts. Example observations: gap between ROK and Japan narrows when using filings/GDP compared to raw resident filings; US has higher resident filings than China and Russian Federation raw, but when normalized by GDP China and Russia have higher filings/GDP. Many countries' 2006 filings/GDP lower than 2000 due to faster GDP growth than filings; exceptions include China and ROK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resident patent filings per million population (per-capita normalization)
rubrics_metrics.description: Resident patent filings normalized per million population (for comparability across countries of different population sizes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to compare patenting intensity on a per-capita basis. Charts presented for 2000 and 2006 show country-level shifts; interpret alongside other normalization metrics (e.g., filings/GDP).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caveat on top-applicant-based statistics
rubrics_metrics.description: Statistics based on subsets of applicants (e.g., top 3,000 PCT applicants) may bias sectoral distributions and counts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: distribution of PCT filings by sector is based on top 3,000 applicants; this excludes individual filers and applicants with <5 filings and may overstate the business sector share. Users should account for this selection when interpreting sectoral breakdowns and top-applicant rankings.
